# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

Quotation guidance:

"""
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.
"""

Resolved Swedish composition guidance (target language):

"""
Swedish is a V2 language: the finite verb is the second constituent of a main clause, so fronting anything at all pushes the subject behind the verb. Write *I morgon åker vi till Malmö*, never *I morgon vi åker till Malmö*. This is the single most common structural tell of a text drafted in English and rendered into Swedish.

Compounds are written as one word. *Kvalitetssäkring*, *kundtjänstmedarbetare*, *miljökonsekvensbeskrivning*. Splitting them is not a stylistic choice in Swedish and often changes the meaning outright — *en rökfri miljö* and *en rök fri miljö* are different claims. Where a compound grows unreadably long, rewrite it into a prepositional phrase rather than splitting it.

Definiteness is marked twice. An adjective before a definite noun takes both the front article and the noun's suffix: *den nya rapporten*, *det stora huset*, *de svenska kunderna*. English has one article and drafts translated from it routinely lose one of the two Swedish markers.

The s-passive is the ordinary Swedish passive and is shorter than its periphrastic alternative: *rapporten skickas på fredag*, not *rapporten blir skickad på fredag*. Both exist; the s-form is the unmarked one, and the *bli*-form carries a change-of-state reading that is often not intended.

*Du* is the default address in Swedish prose, including business and journalism. *Ni* to a single reader is either archaic or a deliberate distancing, and reads as a translation from a language that has a formal pronoun.

*Man* is a fallback rather than the ordinary generic pronoun. It is justified where the agent genuinely is anybody at all or is genuinely unknown, and where naming one would claim more than the material carries. Where the sentence has a real subject to hand — the reader, the writer, the organisation, the profession, the study — that subject is what the sentence takes. A text that reaches for *man* with any of those available reads as evasive, and it is usually where an English draft's *you*, *we*, or passive has landed rather than anything the writer chose.

Speech that the text reports is ordinarily set with a speech dash rather than in quotation marks: an interview answer, a remark at a meeting, anything a person said that the text renders readable. A writer reaches for quotation marks where the phrasing itself is the point — where it is what is new, where it is disputed, or where the text is about how the thing was said. What each of the two marks promises a reader, and what that makes each of them a claim about, is settled in Mechanics; this scope says only which one an ordinary Swedish text reaches for first.

Genitive takes a bare *s* with no apostrophe: *Kntnts kunder*, *Sveriges riksdag*. A name already ending in *s*, *x*, or *z* takes nothing at all: *Anders bok*, *Marx teori*.

Swedish tolerates a shorter sentence than English does and punishes subordination harder. Prefer a main clause with a fronted adverbial to a long relative construction, and prefer a verb to a nominalisation: *när kommunen beslutade* over *vid kommunens beslutsfattande*.

Reach for the established Swedish term where one exists and the field actually uses it — *återkoppling*, *underlag*, *avstämning* — but do not purge the loanwords a professional reader expects. A text that writes *dator* and *webbplats* naturally is Swedish; a text that hunts down every English term and replaces it with a coinage nobody says is not.

Maya Lind är arbetsledare i underhållsteamet och har svarat på frågor via mejl. Hon beskriver vad teamet ville uppnå:

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

- Smallest repair: "… och hur hon skulle planera tiden för förberedelserna inför nästa hus." (This merges with the F2 repair.)

**F4 (minor). "emails" narrowed to emailed fault reports.**
- Draft: "Tidigare sparades felanmälningar som kom per telefon och per mejl var för sig."
- Source: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
- Case: the emails were staff correspondence about work in progress, not residents' reports. This is compatible with "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information", and no supplied statement excludes it. In that case the source holds and the draft's "felanmälningar … per mejl" fails.
- Smallest repair: "Tidigare sparades telefonanmälningar och mejl var för sig."

- Draft heading: "Svale satte upp loggen och utbildade personalen"

- Smallest repair: "Svale satte upp loggen och utbildade sex medarbetare".

- Draft: "anteckningen avstår uttryckligen från att koppla skillnaden till programvaran"
- Source: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software"
- Case: the note reports that the shorter time coincided with the trial (a link) but explicitly does not attribute it to the software (no causation). The source holds and the draft's "refrains from linking" fails. The note's own trial-versus-previous-period comparison is already such a link.
- Smallest repair: "anteckningen tillskriver uttryckligen inte programvaran skillnaden" (this matches the draft's own heading).

**F7. Heading makes larger repairs the determinant of the decision.**
- Draft heading: "Större reparationer avgör fortsättningen"
- Source: "the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
- Case: the team checks how the categories work for larger repairs and then decides on other grounds, such as cost or workload. The source holds; "avgör" fails. The source gives a timing condition and the team as the agent.
- Smallest repair: "Teamet beslutar efter att ha prövat kategorierna på större reparationer", or "Beslutet väntar på hur kategorierna fungerar för större reparationer".

None.

There are no editorial questions and no translation findings.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.
"""

Resolved Swedish composition guidance (target language):

"""
Swedish is a V2 language: the finite verb is the second constituent of a main clause, so fronting anything at all pushes the subject behind the verb. Write *I morgon åker vi till Malmö*, never *I morgon vi åker till Malmö*. This is the single most common structural tell of a text drafted in English and rendered into Swedish.

Compounds are written as one word. *Kvalitetssäkring*, *kundtjänstmedarbetare*, *miljökonsekvensbeskrivning*. Splitting them is not a stylistic choice in Swedish and often changes the meaning outright — *en rökfri miljö* and *en rök fri miljö* are different claims. Where a compound grows unreadably long, rewrite it into a prepositional phrase rather than splitting it.

Definiteness is marked twice. An adjective before a definite noun takes both the front article and the noun's suffix: *den nya rapporten*, *det stora huset*, *de svenska kunderna*. English has one article and drafts translated from it routinely lose one of the two Swedish markers.

The s-passive is the ordinary Swedish passive and is shorter than its periphrastic alternative: *rapporten skickas på fredag*, not *rapporten blir skickad på fredag*. Both exist; the s-form is the unmarked one, and the *bli*-form carries a change-of-state reading that is often not intended.

*Du* is the default address in Swedish prose, including business and journalism. *Ni* to a single reader is either archaic or a deliberate distancing, and reads as a translation from a language that has a formal pronoun.

*Man* is a fallback rather than the ordinary generic pronoun. It is justified where the agent genuinely is anybody at all or is genuinely unknown, and where naming one would claim more than the material carries. Where the sentence has a real subject to hand — the reader, the writer, the organisation, the profession, the study — that subject is what the sentence takes. A text that reaches for *man* with any of those available reads as evasive, and it is usually where an English draft's *you*, *we*, or passive has landed rather than anything the writer chose.

Speech that the text reports is ordinarily set with a speech dash rather than in quotation marks: an interview answer, a remark at a meeting, anything a person said that the text renders readable. A writer reaches for quotation marks where the phrasing itself is the point — where it is what is new, where it is disputed, or where the text is about how the thing was said. What each of the two marks promises a reader, and what that makes each of them a claim about, is settled in Mechanics; this scope says only which one an ordinary Swedish text reaches for first.

Genitive takes a bare *s* with no apostrophe: *Kntnts kunder*, *Sveriges riksdag*. A name already ending in *s*, *x*, or *z* takes nothing at all: *Anders bok*, *Marx teori*.

Swedish tolerates a shorter sentence than English does and punishes subordination harder. Prefer a main clause with a fronted adverbial to a long relative construction, and prefer a verb to a nominalisation: *när kommunen beslutade* over *vid kommunens beslutsfattande*.

Reach for the established Swedish term where one exists and the field actually uses it — *återkoppling*, *underlag*, *avstämning* — but do not purge the loanwords a professional reader expects. A text that writes *dator* and *webbplats* naturally is Swedish; a text that hunts down every English term and replaces it with a coinage nobody says is not.

A term carried into another language names the same thing only where nothing in this context could fall under one term and not the other. Where the two differ, test both directions: name a concrete case, compatible with the supplied material, in which one statement holds and the other fails. The case need only be compatible with the supplied material; the material need not describe it or make it likely. Set a case aside only by quoting a supplied statement that excludes it. If a case stands, that is a finding, however natural or cautious the draft’s wording; if you can name none, it is not. Byline "Av Thomas Barregren" is excluded by instruction (it comes from the invocation, not the material).

## 1. Claim accounting

Each row gives the draft passage, the source passage it rests on (verbatim, English), and what differs.

### Title and lead

| # | Draft | Source | Difference |

| T1 | "Samlad bild av felanmälningar hjälper, säger arbetsledaren" | "Having one view of the reports helps us" (Lind, quotation 3); "maintenance supervisor Maya Lind" | Attribution to the supervisor is correct. Scope differs: the source says the view "helps **us**" (her team). The title drops the object and turns "the reports" into generic "felanmälningar", so it reads as a general claim that a single view helps. **Finding S1.** |
| L1 | "Underhållsteamet på Elm Quay Housing prövade i åtta veckor en gemensam reparationslogg från Svale Systems i två hus." | "its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings"; "It chose Svale Systems"; "The trial lasted eight weeks." | None material. "hus" for "buildings" is the same thing in this context. |
| L2 | "Arbetsledaren Maya Lind berättar vad teamet ville uppnå och hur hon skulle lägga upp förberedelserna en annan gång." | Quotation 1 ("We wanted the evening shift to see…"); quotation 2 ("I would set that time aside before the next building starts."); quotation 3 ("I would leave an extra week for preparation") | Supported. The conditional "skulle" keeps her hypothetical mood. "berättar" is compatible with an email interview. |
| L3 | "En intern anteckning om testet redovisar siffrorna och deras begränsningar." | "Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. ## 2. Findings

### Source-support findings

**S1: Title widens the scope of Lind's assessment (moderate).**
- Draft: "Samlad bild av felanmälningar hjälper, säger arbetsledaren"
- Source: "Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation." Also: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
- Difference: Lind says the single view helps **her team** ("us"), with "the reports" meaning the team's own reports. The title drops "us" and uses the bare plural "felanmälningar", so it reads as her claim that a single view of fault reports helps in general.
- Case where the draft fails and the source holds: the single view helps Elm Quay's two-shift team, but Lind would not claim it helps a housing company with one shift. The material is compatible with this and even points towards it, since she declined to recommend Svale to every housing company. No supplied statement excludes the case.
- Smallest repair: restore the scope, for example "Samlad bild av felanmälningarna hjälper oss, säger arbetsledaren" (or "… hjälper teamet, säger arbetsledaren").

**S2: The lead credits the internal note with figures and limitations the material does not clearly attribute to it (low).**
- Draft: "En intern anteckning om testet redovisar siffrorna och deras begränsningar."
- Source: the note "says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial." The note "explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software." The median times, "The periods had different workloads" and "There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements" are stated without attribution to the note.
- Case where the draft fails and the source holds: the note records the count, the exclusions and its refusal to attribute the difference. The workload remark and the absence of cost, satisfaction and completion measurements come from the case material itself, not from the note. No supplied statement excludes this.
- Smallest repair: attribute only what the note is said to contain, for example "En intern anteckning om testet redovisar antalet anmälningar och vad som inte ingår, och siffrorna från testet har tydliga begränsningar." Or keep the line and treat it as an editorial question to check against the note. The body (B11–B15) is correctly attributed and needs no change.

### Translation findings (quoted speech)

**X1: "innan nästa hus startar" can be misread (low).**
- Source: "I would set that time aside before the next building starts."
- Draft: "Den tiden skulle jag avsätta innan nästa hus startar."
- Obstruction: in a housing-company text, "nästa hus startar" invites the construction reading (byggstart / husstart), which is not what she means. The English "the next building starts" means the next building starts using the log. The Swedish calque keeps the English syntax, so the idiomatic reading goes astray. Meaning, conditional stance and certainty are otherwise intact.
- Smallest repair: "… innan vi börjar i nästa hus." This makes her own team, the referent of the surrounding "Vi", the subject. It leaves open, as the source does, whether "next building" means the trial or a rollout, and it adds no fact. Quotations Q1 and Q3 have no obstruction.

## 3. Completion status

Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, lead, headings, body, quotations, link and publisher line has been accounted for against the source, along with the pronoun features. Unresolved findings: S1 (title scope, moderate), S2 (note attribution in lead, low; may instead be settled as an editorial question against the note itself), X1 (quotation idiom, low). No finding concerns causation, completion time, cost, resident satisfaction, the customer's reservation or the description of the link. All of these are supported as written.
